label: text
content: I pray, forgive my Rudeness in deferring so long my Answer to your obliging Letter, of which some accidental Interruptions, together with my late Indispositions of Health, have been the Occasion. I should very gladly comply with your Request, in giving you such poor Assistance as I am able, towards the Direction of your Studies, but cannot so well do it at this Distance, and upon that little Knowledge I have of you, unless you will be pleased to let me know what your Education has hitherto been in the Way of Learning, what Progress you have made in it, what Languages you understand besides your own, that so I may know what Books you are capable of reading, and withal what your Design is, and what Sort of Books they are that you would read, whether such as serve only to the Promotion of Christian Life and Practice, or such as tend more immediately to the Illumination of your Mind, and the Improvement of your Reason and Understanding in the Way of Science and Speculation. If you please, Madam, to give me some few necessary Hints concerning these Things, that I may not be altogether in the dark in what I have to do, you shall receive my Instruction and Advice. In the mean time, you have the Prayers and best Wishes of

label: abstract
content: Since we are rational Creatures, whose greatest Happiness consists in the perfect Contemplation of Truth and Love of Good; I think it concerns us most to apply our Thoughts to those Things that tend to the Improvement of our Reason, and to the Regulation of our Manners. The former as our best Learning, and the latter as our best Wisdom. As for what the World calls Learning, which consists rather in the Furniture of the Memory, and Force of the Imagination (such as Knowledge of Matters of Fact, History, Languages, great Reading, &c.) than in any clear intellectual Sight of Things, though I do not exclude, yet I would not much commend it, as not understanding the great Value of it, or how it contributes to the Accomplishment of a reasonable Soul, whose greatest Learning must needs lye in the most perfect Habit of Thinking, and whose best Study must consequently be that, which best serves to give her that Perfection. Among which the first I would commend to you, is l'Art de Penser *, both for the Value of the Book, and the Subject it treats of, which is Logick. The next that I would have you read, shall I say, or study, as that which lays the Foundation of all Science, and will best conduct and methodize your Thoughts, is Malebranche's Recherche de la Verité †. This I say, I would commend next, but that in Order to your reading him with Pleasure or Advantage, it is absolutely necessary, you should understand the Cartesian Philosophy, whereof Malebranche is a Superstructure and Improvement. Descartes therefore you must next undertake (after some Competency in the Principles of common Geometry) beginning at his Metaphysical Meditations, thence proceeding to his Principles, and after that as you please in the rest of his Works. A most excellent Book, Poiret's Cogitationes Nationales, and his l'Oeconomie Divine, a great and noble System. The Port Royal's Morality of the New Testament. The Moral Essays of M. Nicbole. Dr. Allefree's Sermons, not so much for their Exactness, as for the natural Flame of Wit, and Spirit of Devotion that shines in them. Dr. Scott's Christian Life. These I think, may serve for the present, and for some of these, there will be a Necessity of a Language or two, Latin is more difficult, and French will now answer all, which therefore I would have you learn out of Hand. 'Tis the most commanding, and therefore most useful Language at present, and Malebranche alone will abundantly reward all the Pains you shall take in it, which need not be great neither, if omitting the tedious Way of learning the Grammar, you only read over twice or thrice the Particles, then the Verbs, and then proceed to go over the Dialogues, and after that any plain Book with a Translation, by which Way you may be Mistress of French so far, as to read a Book by the Help of a Dictionary, in a Month's time. content: I have perused your Book*, with great Admiration, and I hope not without some Advantage; but the Argument being too sublime for my weak Capacity, I dare not presume to give my Opinion of what so much transcends my Understanding. label: text
content: Need, and I beg your Pardon, for not answering your Letter (for which I thank you) so soon as I should, and indeed as I would, if I had not met with many Hindrances since I received it, which as I remember was no sooner than May Day, though it be dated the 30th of March. You cannot imagine what a Hurry my Life is, and what little Command I have of my Time, which instead of being free and intire for my own Use and the Service of my Friends, is lost and dispersed among a Company of Strangers, to whose importune Visits I am continually exposed, an Unhappiness, which I can more easily lament than remedy, but which my Friends I hope will forgive. As to the Objection, which the learned Person you speak of, is pleased to make against the Theory of the Ideal World, that it supposes Precogitancy in God; I grant it most readily, and 'tis what I contend for as a necessary Requisite to his Operations ad extra, or doing any thing without himself, which cannot be effected without some Preconception of it within, unless you will suppose God to act ignorantly, and without knowing what he does, or is about to do, which is impossible. But then I deny that all Precogitancy is an Imperfection. Indeed

label: paragraph_title
content: 204 Mr. Norris's Answer.

label: text
content: Precogitancy as it signifies a laborious and anxious Fore-thought or Contrivance, such as is accompanied with that intense Application of Mind, which we call Study or Premeditation, this indeed is an Imperfection, and such as results from the Limitedness of Understanding, and consequently cannot agree with the Perfection of an infinite Mind. But as for Precogitancy absolutely considered as it signifies only an Ideal View or Preconception of Things, this is so far from being an Imperfection, that without it, God could neither be what he is, nor do what he has done. Nor is it any Objection against Precogitancy in God in this Sense of the Word, to say, that every Thought of the Divine Nature, is immediately Productive, and that to Think with God is to Act. I grant that Thought in God is immediately Productive in Opposition to any manual Operation, or physical Motion, but not in Opposition to a Fore-thought, which must as Necessity intervene, or mediate. And so again, to Think with God, is the same as to Act. It is true, in this Sense, that God acts by Thought, and not by Motion. But it is not true, in this Sense, that all Thought in God is Action, and so (which I suppose, is what this Objection means) that there is no Thought in God antecedent to Action, or no Fore-thought. For that Thought whereby God acts, and which is indeed his Action, is Thought of Volition, and in this Sense to Think with God is to Act; but then there is another Thought in God which regulates and conducts, and in Order of Nature precedes this Action, and that is Thought of Perception or Idea, and in this Sense to Think with God, is Not the Same as to Act. And this I take

THE continuance of your Kindness to a Stranger, to one who has nothing to recommend her to your Esteem, nothing that can satisfy entitle her to those Encomiums you are leased to give her, raises my Wonder, and I look on it as the Result of an uncommon Gerosity, of a more than ordinary Goodness of Temper: You take Delight in obliging, and estow your Favours with such an indearing sweetness, such an engaging Civility, that 'tis impossible to receive them without being sensibly touched by them; they make a deep Impression on the Mind, and with an agreeable Violence constrain the Persons on whom they are conferred, to become your Debtors, among which Number, I must own my self to be one: Yes, Madam, you have laid so many Obligations on me, that you have put it out of my Power to make you a Requital: I have nothing to offer you in Return but Thanks, and hearty and sincere Acknowledgment, which desire you to accept, as being the only Retribution I am yet capable of making you. The Correspondence you have so obligingly begun, shall (if you please to continue it) prove as lasting as our Lives, and I shall think my self very happy in the Conversation and Friendship of so ingenious a Person. label: text
content: I Return my dear Corinna my humble Thanks for both her obliging Letters, and for the Concern she is pleased to express for me. The Story you heard of our being over-turned by a Waggon had not so much as the Shadow of Truth in it, we were not in the least Danger of any kind throughout the whole Journey. You desire a Description of Mr. Norris, which I'll endeavour to give you. He is a little Man of a pale Complexion, but he has a great deal of Sweetness and good Humour in his Face, attended with an extraordinary Modesty, and a more than common Air of Humility; there seems to be a Reservedness in his Temper, but when you're acquainted with him, you'll find

label: text
content: it only the Result of Thoughtfulness : In a Word, he's a Man whose Conversation is very agreeable, as well as instructive, and as I writ you, one who is very much your Friend. I'll leave you and Mr. — to agree about the designed Match with the Etherial Nymph mentioned in Count Gabalis ; there's but one Thing that will render it difficult, and that is, that his Mistress before she's his Wife must learn a Catechism of his own composing. Now I would willingly know how we shall be able to teach it to an Aerial Lady ? But this Point I leave you to settle.

label: text
content: I assure you, my dear Corinna, your Letter was very welcome to me, because it brought with it the good News of your being past those Dangers which your late Illness threatened you with; I hope your present Complaints will vanish as soon as you've recovered a little more Strength, but I fear you will not be perfectly well till Spring, the warm Weather being necessary to compleat your Cure; but neither that, nor any other thing, can be of use to you, if you're still negligent of your self, if you still keep irregular Hours; you ought to remember that, there's a regard due to your self, as well as to your nearest Relations, and that you cannot without being guilty of a Crime, be careless of your own Life; 'tis a Gift bestowed on you by God, and as such ought to be valued; when he thinks fit to resume it, you must indeed part with it without a Murmur, but till that time, 'tis certainly your Duty to preserve it with all imaginable Care, and I believe your Grandmother loves you too well to expect such Services from you as may endanger it. I'm obliged to you for the Concern you express for my Health; but that Abstinence you fear may prejudice me, is absolutely necessary. The greatest Part of my time is spent in my Closet; there, I meet with nothing to disturb me, nothing to render me uneasy; I find my Books and my Thoughts to be the

label: paragraph_title
content: Lady Chudleigh's Letters. 113

label: text
content: most agreeable Companions, and had I not be time accustomed my self to their Conversation, perhaps I should have been as unhappy as any of my Sex: But now, I thank God, I cannot only patiently, but chearfully, bear a great many Things which others would call Afflictions, Life and Death are Things very indifferent to me; I'm neither solicitous for the one, or afraid of the other; I know my self too well to be flattered into a Belief of my being any way useful to the World; my being out of it would prove no loss to any of my Acquaintance; they would find every where much more valuable Persons, such as would be more capable of serving them, and whose Conversation would be much more Entertaining and Instructive than mine. I cannot help pleasing my self sometimes with the Hopes of shortly leaving a World I've very little Reason to be fond of; the Thoughts of lying down in a silent Grave, of taking Sanctuary in a quiet undisturbed Recess, have something very delightful in them; but when I consider, that it becomes me to conform my Will to that of my Maker, and to think that to be best for me which he judges to be so; I blame my self for giving Way to such Thoughts, and resolve to be sedate and easy under every Circumstance of Life, and to employ my leisure Hours in improving my Mind, in enlarging my Understanding, and in making some Progress in the useful Parts of Learning: Morality has been my chief Study since I saw you; the Essays I've writ, are on Knowledge, Friendship, Life, Death, Humility, Grief, and on several other Subjects; you shall see them if I come to London this Winter, but that I believe I shall not, because

content: I am grieved to hear, you enjoy so little Health, 'tis a Blessing I heartily wish you, and all my other Friends, as being one of the greatest Pleasures of Life; while I had the Happiness of possessing it, I could cheerfully struggle with my Misfortunes, be pleasant in the midst of Storms, and easy without any other Company but my Thoughts and Books; but now my Body sinks under the Pressure, and will not keep Pace with my Mind: Life is what I have for many Years had no Reason to be fond of, and a Grave has appeared to me the happiest and best Asylum; I know 'tis

label: paragraph_title

label: text
content: my Duty to maintain my Post, to keep the Station God has assigned me; this Consideration made me leave Afaton, and 'tis that which keeps me here; when I am fully recovered, I will return to my Home, to my solitary Reeves, and these Think away the remaining Moments of my Life. I am very glad you have had the Advantage of good Conversation. You are happy in Mrs. Bridgman's and her Daughter's desirable Company, when you see them, give them my humble Service and my Thanks for the obliging Concern they are pleased to express for me, which I shall ever look on as a Favour that can never be enough acknowledged. Where, when past Images we find,
By Memory with these combin'd,
She from her Store of fading Sense can move,
And frame no Fancy but of Joy and Love.
Where ev'ry Muse, and ev'ry Grace resides,
The sacred Temple where Apollo hides,
From the prophane, and vulgar Eyes,
His awful Mysteries.
This blooming Garden of the Delian God
Long since I left, new Paths to try;
On rough uneven Ground I trod,
And sought the gloomy dark Abode
Of Wisdom and Philosophy.

label: paragraph_title
content: II.

label: text
content:
From hence escap'd, with Joy to Thee I come,
Thee I re-visit now, my native Home.
That Magick Land no more I'll tread,
Nor drink of those Lethargick Streams,
That with their Poison taint the Blood,
And stop the sprightly Purple Flood;
That upward to the sickly Head
Send lazy Vapours, idle Dreams.
Again I'll taste of the Prophetick Rill,
Which rises fast by the Pierian Hill.
Phæbus all other Nymphs forsook,
To chace Caxtalia, young and fair.
To bathe in her delightful Waves,
All other Waters now he leaves.

label: text
content: He loosens here his Golden Hair, And plunges in the lucid Brook. Once the coy Maid refus'd the Grace, And wou'd not suffer his Divine Embrace. Now wiser grown, no more she'll fly, But clasps the God, and hugs the nai Deity,

label: text
content: As Mariners their Canvas Wings diffend, Leaving the Pole, to every Northern blast; Southward their Courses bend, And th' Artic Circle past, The temperate Zone with Pleasure meet; With Pleasure feel the growing Heat, And as they nearer to him run, Salute the long abandon'd Sun. Thus from the frozen Skies, Where once benumb'd she lay, My Muse to milder Regions flies, And to Parnaffus wings her Way.

label: text
content: Methinks already in my Heart, I feel a secret Warmth arise, Which thence diffus'd to ev'ry vital Part, Glows in my Face, and sparkles in my Eyes

I see the Summit of the Hill,
With Spires of Glory crown'd;
And nearer now I see the Mound,
Such was Apollo's Will,

They made a Kind of Litter, in which they carried Thamires to the Cabin of Polemas, where he was treated with extraordinary Care, and it was soon judged, that his Hurt, altho' dangerous, would be attended with no unhappy Consequences.

label: text
content: The News of this Adventure was soon spread all over the Country, but if every one else was amazed at it, Lypidda was almost struck dead with Sorrow; the Danger in which her dear Thamires lay, reduced her to a Condition which nothing but the tenderest Love could occasion. Sach was her Impatience, that she immediately traversed the Fields, in order to get at the Village which contained all that was most dear to her in the World; but her Strength

label: text
content: The Mutual Inconstancy. 145 not answering to her Impatience, through the Shock which this News gave her, she was obliged to be carried Home in the utmost Agony, and wait two Days before she could recover Health enough to enjoy that Happiness.

label: text
content: Those who have loved very tenderly may imagine what was the Despair of this beautiful Shepherdess, never was any so afflicting: But Love, who without doubt directed all the Incidents of this Story, permitted this Misfortune to make Way for another, which proved to be the Henge upon which the whole Affair turned, for in the mean while a Lover of Lydippa, whose Name was Cafir, enraged to Madness at the tender Sentiments of the Nymph for his Rival, and the Scorn with which she treated himself, resolved by Force to make himself Master of her Charms, and carry her into some distant Country, where his Submission and his Love might at length make her forget the too happy Thamires.

label: text
content: He trusted his Design to one of his Friends, who not only approved it, but also determined to assist and follow him in it. They enquired carefully, and learned the Day and Hour which the fair Lydippa had chosen to go to Cyparissa's Village, and went and waited for her in a little Grove through which she was to pass.

label: text
content: The impatient Lydippa, rather led by Love than guided by Reason, went alone from her House: No Journey ever seem'd so long, the cruel Incertainty which disturbed her, seemed to have given her Wings, and tho' she walked so as almost to put herself out of Breath, the Vol. IV. upbraided

label: text
content: To be short, she soon arrived at the Place where the brutal Cafir had resolved to put his wicked Design in Execution; he had provided himself with two good Horses, and coming up to her, Fair Shepherdess (said He) it is with Regret that I obey the Distates of Love; but this Deity, much stronger than my Reason, obliges me to snatch you away from my happy Rival; come Lydippa, continued he, taking her by the Arm, follow a Lover who adores you, and don't constrain me to make Use of Force, at a Time when nothing can defend you from me.

label: text
content: How, treacherous Caifir! answered the unfortunate Lydippa, darest thou offer me this unjust Violence? Thinkest thou to benefit by thy base Treachery? Both Men and Gods will arm in my Defence. Your Cries will rather provoke my Love than my Anger, replied Caifir, seizing her strongly by the Help of his Friend Arguments and Reasons are impertinent when Love commands Silence.

label: text
content: At these Words he had put his Purpose in Execution if Polemas had not at the Instant arrived in this solitary Place. Some secret Movement of which he knew not the Cause, had for some Days past afflicted this Shepherd with a Languor of which he could not get the better, and a Restlessness before unknown to him, occasioned his seeking Solitude. Alas! Could he imagine that Love would have attacked him from any other Quarter than Cyparissa's? This nevertheless was the Beginning of such an Attack. Polemas left his Cabin in a lucky Hour, after having informed himself of

label: text
content: The Mutual Inconstancy. 147 the State of Thamires's Health, he took the Path to the Grove, through which Lydippa was to pass, as the most agreeable to his solitary Humour; but he was hardly entered upon it, when the repeated Cries of the Shepherdess rouzed him from a profound Sleep; he ran hastily towards her, his Heart knew her before his Eyes; and an inconceivable Fury seized him on Sight of the Violence which was offered to her.

label: text
content: Unjust Cafir, (cried he, advancing) treat with Respect the fair Lydippa, or I shall punish your rash Enterprize as it deserves. Is it by barbarous Violence a Man should seek to make himself beloved? In vain you attempt to restore my Soul to Reason, answered the impetuous Cafir, leave me to perpetrate a Fact which Love authorizes, or if your ill Stars compel you to oppose it, your Death shall soon insure the Success of it. I know no better Way of employing my Life, replied Polemas, than for the Defence of this beautiful Shepherdess, so that since you will listen to nothing but blind Rage, let us see if your Courage be equal to your Rashness.

label: text
content: At these Words, this generous Shepherd rushed in upon Caifir, who received him with the more Boldness, because his own vile Friend joined him in the Fray, but Polemas, whose Address and Strength were very great, managed himself so prudently, that the Efforts of both his Enemies were fruitless, altho' they were arm'd each with a Sword, and our Shepherd had nothing but his Crook. At length, Polemas, grown weary of the Incertitude of this Engagement, advanced upon Caifir with such Violence, that he plunged the Iron of his Sheephook in-

This Victory, which a secret Divinity shared with the Shepherd, had for Witnesses the Eyes of the fair Lydippa. She was so struck with an Accident so extraordinary among the peaceful Shepherds, that she had not the Power to fly: Who knows if even Love did not contribute to the heightening of her Fear.

label: text
content: However that be, Polemas, having no more Enemies to combat, came up to the Shepherdess, and spoke thus, Charming Lydippa, what do I not owe to my happy Delliny? I have protected you from unjust Force, and the Defence of so good a Cause obliged the Gods to strengthen my Arm against this vile Ravisher. Generous Polemas, answered the lovely Lydippa, I owe my All to your Courage, you delivered me from a Misfortune more cruel than Death it self. But if any Thing could contribute to the Heightening of your natural Valour, 'twas no doubt the Desire of rendering Thamires the same Service which he had performed for you in the Person of Cyparissa.

label: text
content: Unjust Shepherdess, cried out Polemas, I had no Thoughts but of you alone on this Occasion, and altho' Thamires has saved my Life in prolonging that of Cyparissa, I swear to you that it was not meer Gratitude which brought me to your Assistance; such Merit, and such Beauty, can they want Aid to engage all the World in your Cause? And is it not to please the Gods to search for Occasions of defending the most perfect of their Works? It is not

label: text
content: Ending these Words, this amiable Couple, whom Love resolved to unite in his most charming Bands, pursued the Path towards the Village of Polemas; where the Death of Cafer, and the Valour of Polemas were soon made public. The Resemblance of this Accident with that of Cyparissa, surprized every one; but nothing ever was so tender as the Thanks of Thamires; these two charming Shepherds who had reciprocally saved for each other all that they held precious in the World, carefled each other so tenderly, that this alone had been sufficient to express their Loves; while Cyparissa and Lydippa, embracing each other, swore an everlasting Friendship.

label: text
content: Mean while the Wound of Thamires being out of Danger, he was soon in a Condition of getting up and going to thank Lydippa, who lodged in Cyparissa's Cabbin, for the vast Disquiet which she had born through his illness; their Conversation was tender, it was passionate; but it was easy to observe in it, on both Sides a certain Constraint, in which Cupid took a secret Pride, resolving to eraze from their Hearts that constant Passion which he himself had formed. How can we be defended from

Cyparissa and Polemas on their Part renewed their Vows,'tis true, with equal Tenderness. Their Tongues kept the Habit, while their Hearts seemed to have loft it. They appeared equally restless, Thamires and Lydippa were wanting to their Pleasures: Even so, all the four sought Opportunities of meeting together, with an Earnestness, of which Friendship was the Pre tence, and Love the real Cause.

label: text
content: Mean while the Feast of Pan arrived. All the Shepherds of the Circumjacent Villages, assembled together to celebrate it by a thousand innocent Pleasures, consecrated to this God: Thamires and Polemas, distinguished themselves upon this Occasion, and divided between them the Prizes appointed for the Conquerors.

label: text
content: At length, the Night being come, a Country Ball crown'd the Diversions of this agreeable Day.

label: text
content: 'Twas in a little Grove, to the Musick of several Pipes, and by the Light of a Multitude of Lamps tied to the Trees, they determined in rutilick Dances to finish their Enjoyments, and in Truth nothing was ever so delightful: Cyparissa and Lydippa shew'd their Activity of Limbs, and the Gracefulness of their Air: But Love who could not suffer this Opportunity to pass without mingling his Delights with it, inspired those two Nymphs with a Design of masquing themselves as others did who were at the Ball.

Lydippa adorned her self with several Knots of Amaranth coloured Ribbons, which was Cyparissa's Colour; and this Shepherdess took in her Turn the Gridelin, which Lydippa was exceedingly fond of.

label: text
content: After this Precaution, which was necessary to prevent their being known, they put on their Masques, and returned to the Ball.

label: text
content: Mean while Polemas and Thamires, who could not live a Moment without the Sight of what they adored, sought for them earnestly; they had no sooner observed them but they went to throw themselves at their Feet; if they had dared to follow their real Inclinations perhaps they had not been deceived as they were.

label: text
content: What Disquiet does. one Moment of your Absence give me, fair Shepherdess? I fear always that some new Misfortunes may ravish from me the sole Good to which my Live is attacked; a secret Impulse made Lydippa blush at the Tenderness of this Discourse.

label: text
content: I am of Opinion, Polemas, answered she to him, that this obliging Protestation which you now make to me, bears no Resemblance to the Lukewarmness which you shewed me but even this Minute.

label: text
content: Oh! charming Cyparissa, replied the Shepherd, What do you reproach me with? I have always loved you with the same Ardor; but I confess to you that I feel at this happy instant the most violent Pangs of Love. All my past Sentiments seem trivial to me, in Comparison of those which you have this Day inspired me with. Yes, fair Shepherdess, continued he, kissing her Hand, I adore you, and only Death shall raze from my Heart a Passion so tender, and Transports so moving. The Shepherdess Cyparissa ought to answer to those passionate Discourses, said she, in a Pet which she could not conceal; but Lydippa ought no longer to listen to what cannot be addressed to her.

label: text
content: In speaking these Words she made her self known to Polemas; the Confusion of the Shepherd was excessive; he was tempted to confirm to Lydippa all that he thought he had said to Cyparissa, but he contained himself as yet; Cruel Shepherdess, said he, looking on her with Eyes full of Love, why have you deceived me, or why have you undeceived me? Lydippa was going to answer, and perhaps the Consequence of this Conversation would at last have discovered the Sentiments of their Souls, but she was taken out to dance.

label: text
content: Mean while Thamires had the same Luck with Cyparissa; the Shepherd, like Polemas, found his Ardour increased. He expressed it with all that Love can dictate to Wit, so that the Nymph repenting of being drawn in to hear Transports, which perhaps she wished only for herself, soon made herself known, and left Thamires.

He sought Polemas, and told what had happened to him, and their Confidence became mutual by the Recital of their Adventures. But to revenge this Piece of innocent Deceit, they resolved to pay them in their own Coin; and therefore withdrawing for a Moment, they changed Cloaths, and returned masquered to the Ball. During this Time, the two Shepherdesses told each other the Effects which their Disguises produced; nevertheless, by an equal Impulse of Envy, they strove to conceal from each other some Part of the Raptures which they had observed.

label: text
content: But at length they began to fear left Polemas and Thamires might be offended with this light Raillery, and therefore resolved to appease them; in order to which, they sought them out in their Turn, and had not much Difficulty in finding them: The fair Lydippa advancing to Polemas, whom she mistook for Thamires, and placing her self before him, Oh! my Shepherd, said she, have you forgiven me a Frolick which occasioned the confounding Cyparissa and Lydippa? Ah! Thamires, pursued she, if you loved me now with so strong a Passion as you formerly did, could your Heart commit the Mistake? Would not yours by the Force of Sympathy have discovered which was the real Object of its Desire, in Spite of the Disguise which imposed upon your outward Senses?

label: text
content: Lovely Lydippa, answered Polemas, disguising his Voice, cease to accuse me of an Error, which might have informed you of the Excess of my Love, you might have learned from your charming Companion the Liveliness of my Protestations, and the Excess of my Transports:

A certain imperceptible Power would still draw me towards you, and I well perceive, that to you is attacked all the good Fortune of my Life.

content: Ah! this is too much, cried out Polemas, pulling off his Masque. Both Love and Fortune forbid me such flattering Hopes, these Words were addressed to the happy Thamires, and the unfortunate Polemas ought to have avoided hearing them.

label: text
content: While he spoke, the fair Lydippa remained immoveable, she knew not which to do, to complain of a Mistake which let Polemas into the Knowledge of some of her Thoughts, or be pleased with a Chance which favoured the Wishes of her Heart; at length, she resolved to leave the Shepherd, without giving him an Answer, and go seek Cyparissa, rather out of an Impulse of Curiosity than Jealousy; for she made no doubt but that the Conversation between her and Thamires, was of a Piece with her own.

label: text

label: text

label: text
content: Ah! my dear Thamires, answered the Shepherd, why did you prevent the same Question which I was going to ask you? What can be wanting to your Happiness, who are beloved by the fair Lydippa? and yet nevertheless you seem to me to be uneasy.

label: text
content: Ah! Thamires, know better the Value of your good Fortune, a happy Marriage is ready to crown your Love, you are preparing to be joined to your Shepherdess in the sweetest Bands, and yet at a Time when all Things conspire to brighten your Fortune, you give your self over, without Cause, to a most restless Anxiety.

content: My dear Polemas, ahswered Thamires, fighting, don't endeavour to look into my Soul, I am my self ignorant of what passes therein; but this transporting good Fortune as you esteem it, which unites me to Lydippa, is at the same Time ready to bind you to Cyparissa; how comes it then that your Heart still fights, and seems to wish for somewhat more? Ought it not to be satisfied with a Felicity which the Gods themselves might envy.

label: text
content: I see plainly, cried Polemas, that our Torments are of such a Nature, that we dare not communicate them, let us keep on both Sides our strange Secrets, and let us leave to Love and to Fortune the Care of concealing them, if we must remain unhappy; or of publishing them if these Divinities favour us. 'Twas in this Manner, these two Shepherds, without declaring any Thing, made each other sensible of their secret Passions, while the two Shepherdesses, laboured to conceal from each other the different Emotions which troubled their Minds. Mean while, Cupid, who intended perfectly to open their Eyes, revived the Country Pleasures, over which this God presided as Sovereign. If he armed the Looks of Lydippa, so as to give inevitable Wounds to Polemas; he placed himself in the Eyes of Cyparissa in order to triumph over Thamires: And by a just Equality he furnished these two Shepherds with Charms the most prevailing to inspire what he had inspired them with.

content: There is a fine fresh Water Lake at Mr. Abbourne's Estate, called the Farry; thro' it runs a large River, and full of Fish, Tortoises and Water Fowl, that affords very good Diversion for shooting from a Canoe softly paddled along by Slaves under a cloudy Sky, thus to pass from one little Island to another; in fine, Multitudes of Game are always in view, wheeling round over your Head, cowering low, swimming upon the Water, diving under, or rising from it with others, standing on the Banks, or wafted along upon little Heaps of Sedge: And thus the Tortoises are carried before you, or upon little pieces of floating Timber; the Expanse of still, clear Water discovering ten thousand Fishes, great and small, beneath you. The Noise of the Water Fowl, with the chattering of those upon the Trees and Hills around you, like harsh Notes to sweeten the Melody of the numerous Songkind warbling every where, made still more sweet by the cooing of the wild Pigeons and murmuring of the Turtles, among those thick shadowing Arches of the Forest that hang over your Head upon the Borders; the lovely Land-skip, all concur to make this Solitude of Pleasure extreamly charming.

content: They have Horses for the Saddle in great plenty of the Spanish breed; abundance of black Cattle that have pastures to feed very fat; are as large, or larger than in many parts of England. And I believe there are few Gentlemen in any Country can shew such numbers of their own as Colonel Gale. Besides, they have plenty of Sheep and Goats; but it must be owned their Flesh is generally not so good as with us, nor will take salt so well in the hot Countries. The delicate Food of their Turtle or Tortoises, weighing 150, or 200l. weight in the Markets almost every Day, and sometimes Manatee. Propitious hear our Vows, and hearing aid

label: text
content: IF I did not believe your good Humour to be equal to your Wit, I should think you banter'd your Friend most unmercifully. I'm sure you would not charge me with a fault I am uncapable of committing, nor accuse me of running away with the Wit of the Town, if you had the same Opinion of me that I have of my self; for I also have hitherto been very much deceiv'd in my own Character, if there's any Body takes me for a Wit. That's a Title as far above my Ambition, as out of my Reach; and I have just the cunning of the Fox to cry four Grapes, when I can't come at them. I must confess I never so sensibly perceive'd the want of Wit as I do now, for it requires such a vast Fund to pay you in your own Coin, and to ballance the Accompts in Epistolary Commerce, that I shall certainly turn Bankrupt, unless you'll give large Credit, or, if need be, charitably forgive great Sums. The Satire against Wit, I remember, was for erecting a Wit-Bank in behalf of the poor Traders to the barren Coast. What advantage it would be to me, who have no Cash to put in, I know not, perhaps it might have furnish'd the Town with a Storehouse, that might have supply'd its wants all this Vacation. But it luckily falls out that in describing the dearth of Wit so ingeniously, you consute your self, as oftentimes the richest Men complain most of Poverty. content: This is the only Day I have had to my. self ever since I wrote to you last, and this I design to spend happily in conversing with you, and in the best Company I shall have while I am in the Country, for which I am obliged to you. I have look'd a little into Mrs. Phillips, and 'tis not the first time I have been wonderfully pleas'd with her solid masculine Thoughts, in no feminine Expression. And I like her the better, because, in my Opinion, her Genius and way of Writing, comes the nearest (of any female Author I have met with) to yours, which I think the best that ever fell within my Knowledge. Her refin'd and rational Thoughts of Friendship (not unlike yours) which is a Subject she very much delights in, show a Soul above the common level of Mankind, and mightily raise my desire of practising what she so nobly describes. I am of Opinion that any Person's Humour and Disposition appears as much or more in their Writings, than in their Conversation; and I would never desire a better Character of any one, than what I could

label: header

label: text
content: learn from their own Pen, where it ran without Restraint, or any particular Byass. And tho' I know nothing of Mrs. Phillips but what I have learnt from her own Poems, I am confident she was discreet, good humour'd, modest, constant, and virtuous, as well as ingenious. Her Country Life is so sweet a Poem, and sprinkled with such profound philosophical Thoughts, express'd in easy poetical Language; or else by a kind of Sympathy it suits so well with my Sentiments and Inclination, that tho' I have read several Poems in more Tongues than one upon the same Subject, yet I don't know where to find a better. But whither am I running? Beyond my Lafte I'm sure; for I'm no more a Critick than a Wit or a Poet, leaving those Studies to such as practise them with more Success. And to a Friend I'll own, that Philosophy would be my darling, if I had either time, or strength, or opportunity, to pursue it with the application that it merits and requires: But I have neither, and therefore among the various noble Subjects, with which Philosophy entertains and improves the most exalted Minds, I shall chuse out one, which came from an Oracle, and in two words contains enough to employ all my idle Hours, which can be spar'd from the necessary Concerns of Life. It is Nosce TeIPSUM, (you understand it without an Interpreter). If the Subject be worthless and barren that's my fault, yet such as it is, I know none so little studied, and none so necessary and useful among all that employ the busy Minds of Men. --- My Humour and my Style exactly agree, and I write this with the most prevailing Passion of my Mind, next to my Esteem for Corinna. label: text
content: SINCE you desire my Thoughts at large concerning Philosophy, you shall have such as not first, but last offer themselves, and if I had more time, perhaps they might be fewer. For the longer I think, the less I know; and when I cast up what I have gain'd by my Philosophical Enquiries, and see what the sum total amounts to, I find my self reduc'd almost to that, Philosophers Poverty, who after all his Study and Pains came to this conclusion, Hoc tantum Scio, quod nihil Scio. I am so very sensible of the weakness of Human Understanding, both from my own Thoughts, and the irreconcilable Opinions and endless Controversies of others, that I have but one sure Refuge to fly to, but one Support to rely upon with any confidence, and that is Revelation. Were it not for this, I believe universal Ignorance would have perpetually overspread the face of the Earth. For whatever the Men of Reason of our Days may boast, I know no better way to learn what natural Reason can do, than from what it does, and to inform our selves of that, we must travel to those unhappy Countries, which never heard of

label: paragraph_title
content: PYLADES to CORINNA.

label: text
content: any such thing as Revelation; and there, if the testimony of all Travellers may be credited, we shall soon find enough to humble our Thoughts of Natural Reason, so much indeed, that some of those poor Wretches, who are sunk lowest, seem hardly distinguishable from Brutes by any thing but Shape. They have the same Faculties with the rest of their Species, and might make the same use of them as far as Nature will go. But how imperfect is that even in those places where Learning has been at the greatest height it could attain, without the improvement of express Revelation. I say express, because I am of their opinion, who think all the Learning of the World was originally owing to some obscure Acquaintance with, or dark Hints from the Writings of Moses, and the divine Dispensations to the Israelites. (But be that matter as it will.) How gross and crude were the most knowing Heathens Notions of the Deity? How fickle their Belief of the Soul's Immortality, and a future State? And how different their Sentiments about what one wou'd think should be easiest known, Man's chiefest Good and supreme Happiness? But not to mention Theories, which some Men are audacious enough even now to contest, How imperfect was their most refin'd Morality, in comparison with what Revelation teaches! So far from the noble Generosity of forgiving Injuries, and doing good to Enemies, that it allow'd Revenge. So far from Meekness and Humility, that it represented Vain-glory and Ambition as the most honourable Qualities. If this be the Condition of Natural Reason, what then is Philosophy good for? Why truly in my esteem nothing more, than as it is subservient to the

label: paragraph_title
content: 32 PYLADES to CORINNA.

label: text
content: the better Understanding of Revealed Truths. This is the only good Use I can make of what little I have, or ever shall have, and I have so mean an Opinion of Human Learning abstractedly consider'd, that I reckon it only as you do, an innocent Amusement, which may serve to pass away some idle Hours now and then more agreeably than impertinent Conversation. Influenc'd by such Considerations as these, I chose my Nosce Teipsum, not as a Subject merely Philosophical, but in its largest extent, comprehending all the Duties of the Christian Religion. For he that rightly knows himself, will never be ignorant of his Duty to God and his Neighbour. And I pitch'd upon it the rather, because I think our most certain Knowledge proceeds from Reflection: And it gives me occasion with great Satisfaction to observe, how exactly Reason and Religion agree in every thing conducive to human Perfection and Happiness. Thus Corinna, at your request, for I can deny you nothing; I have given you the Result of my Philosophy. If you desire a farther account of my Religion, you may find it in Dr. Scot's Christian Life; whom I am more indebted to, and have a greater esteem for, than any uninspired Writer whatsoever. The Philosophy of the Christian Religion, and the Reason of all its Precepts is, in my Apprehension, so clearly taught, and so plainly prov'd in that divine Book, that he must want both Head and Heart, who can read it without being not almost, but altogether a Christian. As to that particular in your former Letter; Whether Angels have the same methods of Reasoning that we have, and their Science and ours be the same; 'tis what I think no Man living
